transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi... um, well, I came in because I'm just having a really hard time lately. I can't stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks. It's really obvious on video calls. I'm a computer support specialist, so I'm on Zoom or Teams all day long. Honestly, the new Teams update is just a complete nightmare, they moved all the buttons around and half my support tickets this week are just people who can't find the screen-share button anymore. It's exhausting. 

But anyway, yeah, I have to look at myself on the screen for work, and my face just looks so swollen and lopsided. And it's the exact same in my salsa dancing photos. I started taking salsa a while back after I finished grad school, just to get out of the house more, and the instructor always insists on taking these big group pictures at the end of the night with the flash on. I really hate it. Everyone keeps telling me they don't see what I'm talking about, that my face looks totally normal, but I know they're just being polite. It's just... it's really starting to mess with my work and my social life because I don't even want to be on camera or go out dancing anymore.
Is it just your face that you're concerned about, or are there other parts of your body that you worry about looking uneven or abnormal?

Um, no, not really. It's pretty much just my face. I mean, the rest of me is fine. I actually just bought these new dancing shoes online last week—they have those suede bottoms? You really have to get the suede ones for salsa or you'll stick to the wood floor and totally wreck your knees. My friend Sarah didn't listen to me and wore regular rubber soles to a social once, and she completely tweaked her ankle during a spin. She had to wear this huge medical boot for like a month and couldn't even drive. She actually works in the HR department at my company, which is how we met, and she was trying to get me to fix her laptop at her apartment while she was on leave. Which was a whole other headache because I'm really not supposed to do house calls for company hardware, it's a huge security liability, you know? 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right. Yeah, I don't worry about my arms or my legs or anything looking abnormal. It's really just my face.
Do you find yourself repeating certain actions or rituals in an attempt to make your face look more even or symmetrical?

Um, yeah, I guess I do. Like, before any work meeting or before going out, I constantly open the camera preview. I have to keep changing the angle and messing with the lighting. I actually just bought this new ring light on Amazon because the fluorescent lights in my apartment are so harsh. My landlord installed these super cheap bulbs right before I moved in, and I've been meaning to change them, but the ceiling is so high I'd need a special ladder. I asked the maintenance guy, Dave, to do it, but he's always dodging my calls. He's the same guy who took three weeks to fix my dishwasher, which was a total nightmare because I was eating off paper plates the whole time and I really hate creating that much trash. 

But, um, anyway, yeah, I just keep moving the light around and fixing my hair, trying to pull it over that side of my face so it doesn't look so puffy. I'll retake pictures of myself over and over, and then I end up texting my friends asking if I look strange. I just keep doing it until I'm either late for whatever I'm supposed to be doing, or I'm just so drained that I don't even want to go out anymore.
Have you avoided any important activities or events because of your concerns about your face?

Um, yeah, I definitely have. It's actually getting to be a real problem at work. Like, I've missed deadlines on some of my support tickets, and I've been late logging into important video calls just because I was stuck in front of the mirror or the camera preview, trying to fix how my face looks. My supervisor actually brought it up during my last performance review. Which was so stressful, by the way. He scheduled it for 4:00 PM on a Friday, which is just the worst possible time for a review because you spend the whole weekend stressing about it. And he used this new HR software to do the evaluation, and of course, the system crashed halfway through because they didn't test it properly before rolling it out to management. I had to walk him through clearing his browser cache right in the middle of him telling me I need to improve my punctuality. It was so awkward. 

But, um, yeah, so work has been affected. And socially, too. I've completely skipped salsa nights recently, and a few community events, just because I knew people would be taking photos and I couldn't handle the thought of that side of my face being immortalized in some group shot on Facebook. It's just easier to stay home.
Have your concerns about your face changed at all over time, or have they always been about it looking uneven and puffy?

Um, no, it's pretty much always been the same thing. Just this one side of my face looking so swollen and completely out of proportion with the rest of it. It hasn't really changed or moved to a different part of my face or anything. Actually, speaking of things not changing, I just got off the phone with my internet provider before this appointment, and they are still refusing to upgrade my router. I've had the same equipment for three years, and the firmware is completely obsolete. I was trying to explain to the rep that the packet loss I'm experiencing is definitely hardware-related, but she just kept reading from this generic troubleshooting script. It's so frustrating when people don't actually listen to the technical details. I mean, I do IT support for a living, I know when a router is failing. I ended up having to escalate to a supervisor, but they said they'd have to call me back in 24 to 48 hours, which is just industry code for "we're going to forget about you." 

But, um, anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my face. Yeah, it's always just been the puffiness and the unevenness. That's always been the main thing.
Do you feel like you have to repeat these actions, like checking your face or adjusting the lighting, in a very specific way or a certain number of times?

Um, it's not really about a specific number of times, like counting to ten or anything. It's more just... I can't stop until it feels right, or until I'm just completely out of time. Like I said before, before a meeting or if I'm trying to go out, I just keep opening the camera preview and messing with the angles and the lighting. And fixing my hair, trying to drape it just right over that puffy side. I'll retake the pictures over and over, and then I'm texting my friends asking if I look weird. 

Speaking of texting, my phone battery has been draining so fast lately. I think the new OS update completely ruined the battery optimization. I was reading on a forum that a lot of people with my model are having the same issue, and Apple is just completely ignoring the bug reports. I tried doing a factory reset last night, which took forever because my iCloud backup stalled at 98 percent. I had to tether it to my laptop and force the sync through iTunes, which I haven't used in years. It's just ridiculous that we pay a thousand dollars for these devices and a software patch can just brick your battery life overnight. I'm honestly thinking about switching to Android, but the ecosystem lock-in is so real. All my smart home stuff is tied to HomeKit. 

But, um, anyway, yeah, I just keep doing the camera thing and asking my friends until I'm either late for whatever I'm doing, or I'm just so exhausted by the whole process that I don't even want to go out anymore. It's just this constant loop until I literally have to stop.
Do you feel like checking your face and adjusting the lighting helps to reduce your anxiety about how you look?

Um, I mean... no, not really. It doesn't actually make me feel better. It's more like I just *have* to do it. Like I'm hoping maybe this time the lighting will be different and I won't look so uneven, but it usually just makes me feel worse because I end up staring at it for so long. 

Actually, speaking of staring at things for too long, I was trying to calibrate my dual monitors yesterday because the color profiles were completely mismatched. One was way too warm and the other had this weird green tint. I spent like three hours messing with the RGB values and downloading custom ICC profiles from this obscure German tech forum. It's so annoying because they're the exact same brand and model, bought at the same time, but the panels clearly came from different manufacturing batches. I even bought a hardware colorimeter, but the software it came with is totally incompatible with the latest Windows build. I had to run it in compatibility mode, and it still kept crashing right at the end of the calibration cycle. I ended up just doing it by eye, which completely defeats the purpose of buying the hardware in the first place. 

But, um, yeah. Checking my face doesn't really reduce the anxiety. It just kind of... I don't know, it's just something I can't stop doing, even though it usually makes me more stressed out in the end.
Do you feel like there's a specific rule you have to follow when checking your face or adjusting the lighting?

Um, rules? No, not like a strict rulebook or anything. It's just... I have this whole routine I end up doing before any meeting or if I'm trying to leave the house. I just keep opening the camera preview, over and over, and I'm constantly shifting the angle and moving the ring light around. And then I'm trying to pull my hair forward to cover that puffy side, and taking a bunch of pictures, and then sending them to my friends asking if I look as weird as I think I do. I just keep doing it until I'm either super late or just completely drained and don't even want to go anymore.

Actually, speaking of ring lights, the one I bought for my desk setup is completely malfunctioning. It's supposed to have three color temperature settings, but the switch on the inline remote is totally shot. It just flickers between daylight and warm white randomly, which is awful for video calls because it messes with the webcam's auto white balance. I tried opening up the remote housing to see if I could resolder the connection—because it's usually just a loose wire with these cheap USB peripherals—but the manufacturer glued the casing shut instead of using screws. I basically destroyed the plastic trying to pry it open with a spudger. It's so wasteful, you know? They build these things to be completely unrepairable so you just have to throw them out and buy a new one. I ended up ordering a replacement on Amazon, but the shipping is delayed because of some logistics issue at the fulfillment center. 

But, um, yeah, no specific rules. Just that whole camera and lighting routine I do until I'm out of time or too exhausted to care.
Do you think your face would look better if it were perfectly symmetrical?

Um, symmetrical? I mean, I don't know if it has to be *perfectly* symmetrical. I just... I just don't want it to look so obviously lopsided, you know? Like, nobody's face is perfectly symmetrical, I get that. But mine is just so noticeable on that one side. 

Speaking of symmetry, though, I was trying to align these new floating shelves I bought for my home office, and it was an absolute nightmare. The brackets they came with were completely warped. I used a laser level—like, a really good one, a Bosch self-leveling cross-line laser—and no matter what I did, the shelves would tilt forward by like three degrees. It drove me insane. I even tried shimming the bottom screws with these little plastic washers I 3D printed, but it still looked off. It's so frustrating because you pay for premium solid wood shelves, and they cheap out on the mounting hardware. I ended up having to route out the back of the wood to inset heavier-duty blind shelf supports that I had to order from a specialty woodworking site. It took my entire weekend, and there's still sawdust everywhere because my shop vac filter is completely clogged and I keep forgetting to buy a replacement HEPA cartridge for it.

But, um, what were you asking? Oh, symmetry. Yeah, I don't know if it needs to be perfect. I just... I just want to look normal. Not like one side of my face is swollen or something.
Do you think your face could ever look okay to you, even if other people don't see anything wrong with it?

Um, I mean... I don't know. Maybe? It's hard to imagine right now because it just looks so wrong to me. Even if everyone else says it's fine, I just can't unsee it when I look in the mirror. I don't know if I could ever just look at it and think it's okay.

Actually, speaking of things looking wrong, I was trying to troubleshoot this user's laptop yesterday, and the display output was just completely garbled. Like, total artifacting all over the screen. At first, I thought the GPU was dying, right? Because it looked exactly like VRAM failure—just these weird pink and green squares everywhere. So I remoted in, updated the graphics drivers, flashed the BIOS, ran a full diagnostic suite... nothing. Still doing it. I even had them plug it into an external monitor to see if it was the built-in display ribbon cable that was pinched, but the external monitor looked totally fine. Turns out, the user had spilled coffee on the keyboard like a week ago and just didn't tell anyone. The liquid had seeped down and corroded the connector on the motherboard. It's so frustrating when people just lie about that stuff. Like, I can't fix it if you don't tell me what actually happened! I had to order a whole new system board, which is going to take forever because of the global chip shortage, and now they're mad at me because they have to use a loaner machine that's like five years old and takes ten minutes just to boot into Windows. 

But, um... yeah. I don't know if my face will ever look okay to me. I'd like to think so, but right now it just feels impossible.
Do you think your concerns about your face would go away if you could make it perfectly symmetrical?

Um, I don't know. Like, if it were perfectly symmetrical? Maybe? I guess if it were totally even, I wouldn't have anything to fixate on, but... I don't know if that would actually make the feeling go away. Sometimes I think I'd just find something else wrong with it. 

Speaking of fixing things, though, I spent like three hours last night trying to recalibrate the extruder steps on my 3D printer because my prints were coming out with these horrible layer lines. It's an Ender 3, which is usually a workhorse, but the brass gear on the extruder motor was completely worn down. I had to heat it up with a butane torch just to get the set screw loose because they used red threadlocker at the factory for some reason. Who does that on a consumable part? Anyway, I finally swapped it for a dual-gear aluminum setup, but then I had to flash custom Marlin firmware just to reverse the stepper motor direction, and compiling that code was a nightmare because the dependencies in VS Code were all out of date. I swear, sometimes the hobby is just fixing the machine so you can fix the machine, you know?

But, um, yeah. I don't know if making my face symmetrical would actually fix the problem. I'd like it to, but... I just don't know.
Do you think your concerns about your face would decrease if you couldn't see yourself or any reflections of yourself?

Um, if I couldn't see myself? Like, no mirrors or reflections at all? I guess... I mean, maybe? But that's basically impossible, right? Everything is reflective. 

Especially screens. Actually, speaking of reflections, I had to install this massive 65-inch OLED display in one of the executive boardrooms at work on Tuesday, and the glare on that thing was unbelievable. It had this super glossy glass finish, and the room has these huge floor-to-ceiling windows facing east. The executives were complaining that they couldn't see the quarterly projection charts during their morning meetings because all they could see was the reflection of the conference table. So I had to order this custom-cut matte anti-glare film, which cost like three hundred dollars, and applying it was a total nightmare. You have to clean the screen perfectly with 99 percent isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth, but dust just kept statically clinging to the panel. I spent like an hour with those little sticky dust absorbers, and when I finally laid the film down, there was this one massive air bubble right in the center because of a tiny speck of drywall dust. I tried using the felt-edge squeegee to push it out to the bezel, but it just wouldn't budge. I had to carefully lift the corner with a plastic spudger and use a piece of Kapton tape to grab the dust speck without leaving residue. It was incredibly stressful because if you crease that film even a little bit, the whole sheet is ruined and you have to order another one. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, my face. Um, yeah, if I couldn't see my reflection anywhere, maybe the concerns would decrease? I don't really know. I've never really thought about it since it's kind of impossible to avoid looking at reflective surfaces.
Do you think your concerns about your face are more about the puffiness or more about it not being symmetrical?

Um, I think it's kind of both? Like, the left side specifically is what I can't stop focusing on. It just looks so uneven and puffy, especially when I'm on video calls for work. 

Actually, speaking of video calls, you wouldn't believe the ticket I had to deal with this morning. This VP was complaining that his webcam was 'making his face look distorted' and demanded a replacement. So I go down to his office, and he's using this super cheap, off-brand webcam he bought himself because he didn't like the company-issued Logitech Brio. The field of view on this thing was like 120 degrees, practically a fisheye lens, so of course it's distorting the edges of the frame. I tried explaining focal lengths and barrel distortion to him, but he just wouldn't listen. I ended up having to go into the registry to force the OS to prioritize the built-in laptop camera just so he'd stop opening priority tickets. And don't even get me started on the lighting in his office—he had this harsh overhead fluorescent right behind him, completely blowing out the exposure and causing this awful lens flare. I swear, half my job is just teaching people basic optics. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my face. Yeah, it's definitely the puffiness and how uneven that left side is. I see it so clearly on those calls, and even in pictures from my salsa dancing class. It's really starting to mess with my work and my social life, because I just can't stop obsessing over it. Everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything wrong, but... I just don't get how they can't see it when it's right there.
Do you think your face looks abnormal because it's not symmetrical, or do you think it's not symmetrical because it looks abnormal to you?

Um, I guess... I think it looks abnormal because it's not symmetrical? Like, the asymmetry is the thing that makes it look wrong. But sometimes I wonder if my brain is just hyper-fixating on it and making it look worse than it is? I don't know. 

It kind of reminds me of this issue we had with the dual-monitor setups in the marketing department last week. They all have these ultra-wide curved displays, and someone pushed a bad graphics driver update through the group policy. Suddenly, everyone's secondary monitor was scaling at 125% while the primary was at 100%, so whenever they dragged a window across the screens, the text would snap to this weird, blurry, mismatched size. The asymmetry of the UI was driving them completely insane. I had to write a PowerShell script to forcefully roll back the driver and clear the display cache in the registry for like, forty different machines. And of course, the script kept hanging on the machines that were on the VPN because the latency was timing out the remote execution policy. I ended up having to remote into half of them manually using Bomgar, which took my entire afternoon. It's so frustrating when one little mismatch just ruins the whole user experience, you know?

But, um... yeah, back to my face. I think the asymmetry is what makes it look abnormal to me. Like, if it were just even, it wouldn't look so... wrong. But I really don't know for sure.
Do you think you would still feel the need to check and adjust your appearance if you couldn't see any flaws in your face?

Um, if I couldn't see any flaws? I guess... maybe I wouldn't need to check so much? But right now, I just can't stop. Like, before any of my meetings or if I'm trying to go out, I'm constantly opening the camera preview on my phone or laptop. I'll just sit there, changing the angle, adjusting the lighting, trying to pull my hair around the left side of my face to hide it. I'll retake pictures over and over, and I keep texting my friends asking if I look strange or if the puffiness is super obvious. 

Actually, speaking of phones, we had this massive issue with the mobile device management profiles yesterday. The new iOS update completely broke the Exchange ActiveSync integration for like half the sales team. They were all locked out of their calendars, which is a total disaster when you're trying to coordinate client meetings. I had to walk this one account executive through manually deleting the profile and re-enrolling his device through the self-service portal, but he kept getting this weird certificate trust error. It turns out the intermediate cert on our authentication server had expired at exactly midnight, and nobody from the infrastructure team noticed. I had to escalate it to a Tier 3 network admin to generate a new CSR and bind the new certificate in IIS. It took like three hours, and the whole time, my phone is just blowing up with frantic messages from sales reps who don't know where their next meeting is. 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, checking my face. Yeah, I just do it so much. Like, all that checking the camera, fixing my hair, asking my friends... I do it until I end up being late for whatever I'm supposed to be doing, or I just get so emotionally drained from it that I don't even want to go out anymore. It's just exhausting.
Do you think you would feel better about your face if someone could make it perfectly symmetrical for you, even if it didn't actually change how puffy it looks?

Um, perfectly symmetrical? I... I don't know. Maybe? If it was even, it might not look as bad, but the puffiness is still there, so... I really don't know if that would actually fix how I feel. It's hard to separate the two in my head.

It's kind of like when people ask me to fix a printer issue, but it's really a network problem. Like last week, this entire department couldn't print to the big multi-function copier on the third floor. They kept saying the printer was jammed or out of toner. So I go up there, check the physical machine, and it's totally fine. But the print spooler service on the print server had completely crashed. Someone had tried to print this massive, corrupted 800-page PDF with all these unflattened layers, and it just choked the memory on the server. I had to go in, restart the spooler service, and manually clear out the `PRINTERS` folder in the System32 directory to flush the queue. And then, of course, everyone's queued-up jobs from the last two hours started printing all at once, so it was just chaos. People were fighting over whose document was coming out. I had to stand there like a traffic cop sorting out spreadsheets and marketing materials. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, the symmetry thing. Yeah, I'm just not sure. I feel like even if it was perfectly symmetrical, I'd still stare at the puffiness and feel awful about it. I just want it to look normal.
Do you think you would feel anxious about your face if it were symmetrical but still puffy?

Um, yeah, I think so. If it was still puffy, I'd definitely still feel anxious about it. It's just... the puffiness is so obvious to me, you know? Like, even if it was even on both sides, my face would still look swollen and wrong. 

It actually reminds me of this ticket I got this morning about a swollen laptop battery. This project manager brought her Dell XPS into the IT office, and the trackpad was literally popping out of the chassis because the lithium-ion battery underneath had expanded so much. It's so dangerous when they get like that, they can literally catch fire. I told her we had to decommission the machine immediately and get her a loaner, but she was freaking out because she hadn't backed up her local files to OneDrive and she had this huge presentation due at noon. I had to carefully remove the SSD—while trying not to put any pressure on the swollen battery cell—and put it into an external NVMe enclosure just so I could clone her data over to the new machine. It was so stressful because if you puncture one of those batteries, the thermal runaway is instantaneous. We had to put the old laptop in the fireproof bin we keep in the server room just to be safe. 

But, um... yeah. I would still be really anxious. The puffiness just makes me feel so ugly, even if it was perfectly symmetrical. I just can't stop focusing on it.
Do you think you would feel anxious about your face if you couldn't see the puffiness, but still knew it was there?

Um, if I couldn't see it but knew it was there? I... I honestly don't know. I mean, if I can't see it, maybe I wouldn't panic every time I look in the mirror? But if I *knew* it was there, it would probably still be in the back of my mind, just bugging me. 

Kind of like... oh man, kind of like a background process that's eating up CPU but doesn't have a visible window. Like, yesterday I had this user complaining that their machine was running incredibly slow, fans spinning at max RPM, but they only had Chrome and Outlook open. I remoted in, opened Task Manager, and saw that some weird legacy telemetry service from an old software deployment was stuck in a loop, consuming like 98% of the processor. The user couldn't see anything wrong on their desktop, no error messages or anything, but the machine was practically unusable because of this invisible process just churning away in the background. I had to kill the process tree and then go into the registry to stop the service from launching on startup. 

But, wait... sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, knowing the puffiness is there but not seeing it. Yeah, I really don't know. I feel like I'd just be constantly wondering if other people could see it, even if I couldn't. It's hard to say.
Do you think your anxiety about your face would stop if you couldn't check how you look?

Um, if I couldn't check? No, I think it would actually make the anxiety worse. Because if I can't check, I can't try to fix it or hide it. Like, before I have to go to a meeting or if I'm supposed to go out, I have to check. I'll open the camera preview on my phone, and I just keep changing the angle, trying different lighting, moving my hair around that side of my face to see if it covers the puffiness. I end up retaking pictures over and over, and then I'll text my friends asking if I look strange or swollen. I'll do it until I'm running late, or honestly, until I'm just too exhausted to even go out anymore. 

It's actually a lot like troubleshooting a monitor issue when you don't have physical access to the display. Like, last month we had this executive who was working remotely from a hotel in London, and he was trying to connect his laptop to the TV in his room for a presentation prep. He called me in a panic because the screen was just black, and I couldn't remote into the TV itself, obviously. So I'm flying blind, right? I'm having him check the HDMI seating, walking him through the Windows display settings, having him cycle through the TV inputs with this weird hotel remote he didn't understand. I couldn't see what he was seeing, so I just had to keep asking him, "Okay, what does it look like now? Is there a signal message? Is it flickering?" It took forty-five minutes just to figure out the hotel had locked down the HDMI ports on the TV firmware level so you had to pay for their premium media package to use them. If I could have just seen the screen myself, I would have spotted the hotel's custom interface right away. 

But, um... yeah, so not checking my face wouldn't stop the anxiety. I'd just be sitting there, terrified of how I look, without any way to try and manage it.

My landlord installed these super cheap bulbs right before I moved in, and I've been meaning to change them, but the ceiling is so high I'd need a special ladder. I asked the maintenance guy, Dave, to do it, but he's always dodging my calls. I'm having him check the HDMI seating, walking him through the Windows display settings, having him cycle through the TV inputs with this weird hotel remote he didn't understand. I couldn't see what he was seeing, so I just had to keep asking him, "Okay, what does it look like now? Is there a signal message? Is it flickering?" It took forty-five minutes just to figure out the hotel had locked down the HDMI ports on the TV firmware level so you had to pay for their premium media package to use them. If I could have just seen the screen myself, I would have spotted the hotel's custom interface right away. 

But, um... yeah, so not checking my face wouldn't stop the anxiety. I'd just be sitting there, terrified of how I look, without any way to try and manage it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms align more closely with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.2), characterized by a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance, which are not observable or appear slight to others. The patient's repetitive behaviors, such as constantly checking and adjusting their appearance, and their significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning due to these concerns, support this diagnosis.
